title: Bipolar Transistor Characteristics & DC Operating Point Analysis

content.aim: To determine the DC operating point (Q-point) of a bipolar junction transistor in common-emitter configuration and to examine its terminal current-voltage characteristics. The experiment also investigates the behaviour of the transistor in cutoff, active and saturation regions and examines the effect of emitter resistor on Q-point stability.
objectives: To study the structure and operation of an NPN bipolar junction transistor (2N2222) and its terminal conventions.
To measure the input characteristics (IB versus VBE at constant VCE) using the laboratory trainer.
To measure the family of output characteristics (IC versus VCE for different IB values) and plot them.
To identify the cutoff, active and saturation regions on the output characteristics.
To construct the DC load line and locate the quiescent Q-point from the intersection with the IB curve.
To examine the role of emitter resistor RE in thermal stabilization by comparing the operating point with VS disconnected and with RE shorted.

theory.text:
Bipolar Junction Transistor Structure and Operation

The bipolar junction transistor is a three-terminal device formed by two p-n junctions in a single crystal. In an NPN transistor, a thin, lightly doped p-type base is placed between two heavily doped n-type regions (emitter and collector). Conduction involves both electrons and holes, hence the term bipolar.

• Emitter (E): Heavily doped n+ region. Its function is to inject electrons into the base.

• Base (B): Very narrow (0.5 to 1.5 µm) and lightly doped p-type. The narrow width and light doping ensure low recombination, so most injected electrons diffuse across to the collector. Typically 98% to 99.5% of electrons reach the collector.

• Collector (C): Moderately doped n-type with larger area. It collects the electrons that cross the base and dissipates power PD = VCE * IC, hence the larger physical size for heat removal.

Current Relationships

Applying KCL at the transistor terminals:

\[\mathit{I}_{E} = \mathit{I}_{B} + \mathit{I}_{C}\]

The collector current consists of the injected component and the reverse saturation current ICBO of the collector-base junction:

\[\mathit{I}_{C} = \alpha \mathit{I}_{E} + \mathit{I}_{CBO}\]

\[\alpha = (\mathit{I}_{C} - \mathit{I}_{CBO}) / \mathit{I}_{E} \approx \mathit{I}_{C}/\mathit{I}_{E} \quad (0.95 \le \alpha \le 0.998)\]

In common-emitter configuration, the transistor acts as a current amplifier. Substituting IE = IB + IC:

\[\mathit{I}_{C} = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha} \mathit{I}_{B} + \frac{\mathit{I}_{CBO}}{1-\alpha} = \beta \mathit{I}_{B} + \mathit{I}_{CEO}\]

\[\beta = \mathit{h}_{FE} = \alpha/(1-\alpha) = \mathit{I}_{C}/\mathit{I}_{B}\]

For the 2N2222 at room temperature, ICEO is in the nanoampere range and negligible compared to milliampere operating currents. In the active region:

\[\mathit{I}_{C} = \beta \mathit{I}_{B} \quad (50 \le \beta \le 300)\]

Operating Regions

The bias condition of the two junctions determines the operating region:

• Cutoff: BE junction reverse biased or VBE < 0.5V, CB reverse biased. IB ≈ 0, IC ≈ 0, VCE ≈ VCC. Transistor acts as open switch.

• Active: BE forward biased (0.65-0.75V), CB reverse biased. IC = β IB. This is the linear amplification region.

• Saturation: Both junctions forward biased, VCE(sat) ≈ 0.1-0.2V, IC < β IB. Transistor acts as closed switch, current limited by external resistors.

DC Load Line and Q-Point

With supply VCC, collector resistor RC and emitter resistor RE, KVL around the output loop gives:

\[\mathit{V}_{CC} = \mathit{I}_{C}\mathit{R}_{C} + \mathit{V}_{CE} + \mathit{I}_{E}\mathit{R}_{E}\]

Since IE ≈ IC:

\[\mathit{V}_{CC} = \mathit{V}_{CE} + \mathit{I}_{C}(\mathit{R}_{C}+\mathit{R}_{E})\]

\[\mathit{I}_{C} = -\frac{1}{\mathit{R}_{C}+\mathit{R}_{E}} \mathit{V}_{CE} + \frac{\mathit{V}_{CC}}{\mathit{R}_{C}+\mathit{R}_{E}}\]

This is a straight line on the IC vs VCE plot. Its intercepts are:

• Cutoff (IC=0): \[\mathit{V}_{CE(cutoff)} = \mathit{V}_{CC} = 12.0V\]

• Saturation (VCE=0): \[\mathit{I}_{C(sat)} = \mathit{V}_{CC}/(\mathit{R}_{C}+\mathit{R}_{E}) = 12/1100 = 10.91mA\]

The Q-point is the intersection of this load line with the characteristic curve corresponding to the base current set by the bias network. For undistorted amplification, the Q-point is ideally placed near the centre of the load line.

Role of Emitter Resistor and Thermal Stability

RE provides negative feedback for thermal stability. If temperature rises, IC tends to increase, increasing VE = IE RE. Since VB is fixed by the voltage divider (RB1, RB2), VBE = VB - VE decreases, reducing IB and counteracting the rise in IC. When RE is shorted, this feedback is removed and the operating point shifts significantly, making the circuit prone to thermal runaway.

The voltage divider is designed to be stiff, meaning current through RB1 and RB2 is much larger than IB, so VB remains approximately constant despite variations in IB. Condition for stiff divider is typically Idiv ≥ 10 IB, or RTH ≤ 0.1(β+1)RE. In this experiment, RTH = 12.88kΩ and (β+1)RE = 15.1kΩ, ratio 0.85, moderately stiff. A stiffer divider would use smaller RB1 and RB2 at cost of higher power dissipation.

The DC load line represents all possible operating points for given VCC, RC and RE. Q-point should be centered for maximum symmetrical swing. If too close to cutoff, positive peaks clip; if too close to saturation, negative peaks clip. Measured Q-point at VCE=5.75V, IC=5.25mA is near midpoint of 12V and 10.91mA, providing good headroom for Class A amplifier design.

Early Effect and Output Resistance

In active region, IC is not perfectly constant with VCE due to base-width modulation (Early effect). As VCB increases, collector-base depletion region widens into base, reducing effective base width WB. This increases concentration gradient and reduces recombination, causing slight increase in IC with VCE. Slope corresponds to output resistance ro = ΔVCE/ΔIC. Extrapolated active-region curves intersect voltage axis at Early voltage VA, typically 50-150V for small-signal transistors. For 2N2222, VA≈100V, giving ro≈(VA+VCE)/IC≈20kΩ at 5mA. This finite output resistance limits maximum voltage gain of CE amplifier to -gm*(RC||ro||RL).

Additional Analysis: Thevenin Equivalent and Stability Factor

The base bias network formed by RB1 and RB2 can be represented by Thevenin equivalent VTH = VCC * RB2/(RB1+RB2) and RTH = RB1||RB2. For this experiment, VTH = 1.70V and RTH = 12.88kΩ. The base-emitter loop equation is VTH = IB RTH + VBE + IE RE. Since IE ≈ IC = β IB, the collector current can be expressed as IC = (VTH - VBE)/(RE + RTH/(β+1)). This shows dependence on β is reduced when RTH/(β+1) << RE, which is condition for stiff divider. Stability factor S = dIC/dICO is also improved by RE. Without RE, S ≈ β+1, large and unstable. With RE, S = (1+β)/(1+β*RE/(RE+RTH)) which is much smaller, improving thermal stability.

Thermal runaway occurs because VBE decreases -2.2mV/°C and β increases with temperature, causing IC to increase, increasing power dissipation VCE*IC, raising junction temperature further. RE provides negative feedback to counteract this. In this experiment, shorting RE removed feedback and IC increased from 5.25mA to 9.55mA, demonstrating loss of stability. In practical power transistors, thermal runaway can destroy device if not properly heatsinked and stabilized.

Error Analysis

Measured IC = 5.25mA versus calculated 5.40mA, error 2.8%. Sources of error include: resistor tolerance (5% carbon film resistors used in lab, so RB1, RB2, RC, RE can vary ±5%), DMM accuracy (±0.5% for voltage, ±1% for current), meter loading (DMM input impedance 10MΩ loads divider slightly), temperature variation (lab temperature ~28-30°C versus 25°C standard, affecting VBE), and contact resistance of breadboard and banana wires. VCE error 5.11% also within expected range for undergraduate lab with standard equipment. These errors are acceptable and do not affect conclusions.

Design Considerations for Linear Amplifier

For Class A amplifier, Q-point should be centered on load line to allow maximum symmetrical swing without clipping. If Q-point too close to cutoff, positive half-cycle clips; if too close to saturation, negative half-cycle clips, causing distortion. Centered Q-point at VCE≈VCC/2 gives maximum unclipped output. In this experiment, VCC=12V, so ideal VCE≈6V, close to measured 5.75V, giving good headroom. RC and RE values also affect gain and stability. Larger RC gives higher voltage gain Av≈-RC/re but reduces VCE headroom and increases saturation risk. Larger RE improves stability but reduces gain if unbypassed and reduces output swing. Bypass capacitor CE can be used to bypass RE for AC signals, increasing AC gain while maintaining DC stability, as studied in EEE 302.

The Early effect causes finite output resistance ro = VA/IC, where VA is Early voltage. For 2N2222, VA≈100V, so ro≈20kΩ at 5mA. This limits maximum voltage gain to -gm*(RC||RL||ro). In this experiment, RC=1kΩ, so RC||ro≈0.95kΩ, close to RC, so Early effect has small effect on gain but explains slight slope in output characteristics in active region.

procedure: The TPS-3371 trainer was connected to the regulated DC supply. The supply was switched OFF and controls turned down before wiring. The 2N2222 NPN transistor was inserted into the breadboard socket after confirming the E-B-C pin configuration from the datasheet.

Circuit 1 was wired as shown in Schematic 1: RB1 = 91kΩ between +12V and base, RB2 = 15kΩ between base and ground, RC = 1.0kΩ between +12V and collector, and RE = 100Ω between emitter and ground. The variable source VS was connected to the input node. Connections were checked to avoid short circuits.
The power supply was switched ON and the main rail adjusted to +12.00V as measured with a digital multimeter. The multimeter was set to high input impedance mode to avoid loading the divider.

VS was varied from 0.1V to 1.2V in 0.1V steps. At each step, VB, VC and VE were recorded. From these, VCE = VC - VE, VBE = VB - VE, IE = VE/RE and IC = (VCC - VC)/RC were calculated and tabulated as in Table 301.1.

IC was plotted against VCE to obtain the common-emitter output characteristics. The DC load line joining VCE = 12V (IC=0) and IC = 10.91mA (VCE=0) was drawn and the cutoff, active and saturation regions were marked.

Circuit 2 (VS disconnected): The variable source was completely removed, leaving the self-biased voltage divider. The quiescent voltages VB, VC, VE were measured, IC was calculated and the Q-point was marked on the load line. This represents normal self-biased operation.

Circuit 3 (RE shorted): The supply was switched OFF, a low-resistance jumper was placed across RE to short it, and the supply was switched ON again. VB, VC, VCE were re-measured and the new IC = (VCC - VC)/RC was calculated. The shift in operating point was noted to observe the effect of removing emitter feedback, as recorded in Table 301.2.
precautions: The transistor pinout was confirmed before applying power. Interchanging collector and emitter results in reverse active operation with very low gain and possible breakdown.
Collector power dissipation VCE * IC was kept below the 2N2222 rating of 500mW at 25°C. In this setup maximum dissipation was about 31.5mW, within safe operating area.
The DC supply was switched OFF before changing jumper connections, especially when shorting RE, to prevent accidental shorting of the +12V bus and blowing the supply fuse.
Multimeters were set to high input impedance (≥10MΩ) so that measurements at the base node did not load the 91kΩ/15kΩ divider and cause erroneous VB readings.
A short delay was allowed between voltage adjustments for junction temperature to stabilize before recording readings, as VBE is temperature dependent.
content.discussion:
The measurements obtained for the 2N2222 transistor are consistent with standard BJT theory, with minor deviations attributable to component tolerance and measurement limitations.

Input Characteristics: The base-emitter junction behaved like a forward-biased diode. Below VBE ≈ 0.5V, IC was less than 0.05mA and the transistor remained in cutoff. Beyond the knee voltage around 0.65V, base current increased rapidly and collector current followed proportionally. This exponential behaviour was evident in Table 301.1, where VBE remained relatively constant around 0.65-0.73V while IC rose from 0.02mA to 10.98mA as VS increased from 0.3V to 1.2V.

Output Characteristics: Three regions were clearly observed on the IC vs VCE plot:

• Cutoff: At low VS, IB ≈ 0, IC ≈ 0, VCE ≈ 12V. The transistor presents high impedance between collector and emitter. This was seen in steps 1-3 where VC remained near 12V and VE near 0V.

• Active: From VCE ≈ 1.0V to 12V, the curves were largely flat with a slight positive slope. This slope is due to the Early effect (base-width modulation) where increasing VCE widens the collector-base depletion region, reducing effective base width and slightly increasing β and IC. The measured slope corresponds to output resistance ro ≈20kΩ.

• Saturation: When VCE fell below 0.3V (steps 11-12), IC became limited by external resistors rather than base current: IC(sat) ≈ (VCC - VCE(sat))/(RC+RE) ≈ 10.77mA, close to the measured 10.98mA. In this region VCE(sat) was 0.07V and 0.02V, typical for saturated silicon transistor.

Bias Stability and Role of RE

For Circuit 2 (VS disconnected), the Thevenin equivalent of the base divider is:

VTH = VCC * RB2/(RB1+RB2) = 12 * 15/(91+15) = 1.70V
RTH = RB1 || RB2 = 12.88kΩ

KVL around base-emitter loop: VTH = IB RTH + VBE + IC RE

IC = (VTH - VBE)/(RE + RTH/(β+1))

With VBE = 0.70V and β ≈ 150, IC(calc) = (1.70-0.70)/(100+85.3) = 5.40mA. The measured value was 5.25mA, a difference of 2.8%. This small deviation is attributable to 5% resistor tolerance, meter loading and temperature variation. VCE(calc) = 12 - 0.0054*1100 = 6.06V versus measured 5.75V, error 5.1%, also within expected tolerance.

When RE was shorted (Circuit 3), the feedback term IE RE was removed. Base current increased to:

IB = (VTH - VBE)/RTH = (1.70-0.72)/12.88k = 76.1µA

IC rose to 9.55mA, an increase of about 82%, and VC fell to 2.45V. The Q-point shifted close to saturation with VCE=2.45V. Without RE, any rise in temperature would reduce VBE by about -2.2mV/°C and increase β, causing further rise in IC without compensation, leading to thermal runaway. This demonstrates why emitter resistor is standard in practical biasing for thermal stability, even though it slightly reduces AC gain if unbypassed.

The experiment also confirms the importance of stiff voltage divider design. If RTH is not much smaller than (β+1)RE, the Q-point becomes dependent on β spread, which can vary from 100 to 300 for same transistor type. In this circuit, the divider is moderately stiff, giving reasonable stability.

Overall, the load line, Q-point and stability concepts were verified experimentally and align with theoretical calculations within acceptable error margins for undergraduate laboratory measurements.

content.conclusion:
The experiment verified the fundamental operation of a bipolar transistor in common-emitter configuration. The input characteristic showed exponential diode behaviour with knee voltage around 0.65V. The output family clearly displayed cutoff, active and saturation regions. The DC load line was established between VCE(cutoff)=12.0V and IC(sat)=10.91mA, with measured Q-point at VCE=5.75V, IC=5.25mA near centre of load line, suitable for linear amplification. Comparison of self-biased circuit and RE-shorted circuit confirmed that RE provides negative feedback that stabilizes operating point against temperature and β variations. Removing RE caused IC to increase by over 80% and shifted transistor toward saturation, confirming its importance in practical bias design.

questions.question: Compare between the preliminary questions / theoretical examples and the measurement results obtained in the laboratory.
questions.answer: Theoretical: VTH = 1.70V, RTH = 12.88kΩ. With VBE=0.70V and β=150, IC(theoretical) = (1.70-0.70)/(100+85.3) = 5.40mA, VCE(theoretical) = 12 - 0.0054*1100 = 6.06V. Experimental (Circuit 2): IC = (12.00-6.75)/1000 = 5.25mA, VCE = 6.75-1.00 = 5.75V. Error in IC = (5.40-5.25)/5.40*100 = 2.78%, error in VCE = (6.06-5.75)/6.06*100 = 5.11%. Errors within 6% and attributable to resistor tolerance (5%), meter loading and temperature. Agreement is good for undergraduate lab.

questions.question: Clearly identify, mark, and mathematically delineate the three operating regions on the output characteristic graph.
questions.answer:
• Cutoff: Region below IB=0 curve, near horizontal axis. Condition: VBE < 0.6V, IC ≈ ICEO ≈ 0, VCE ≈ VCC. Transistor OFF, open switch. Observed at steps 1-3 where VC≈12V.
• Active: Central region where curves are flat and evenly spaced. Condition: VCE ≥ VCE(sat) ≈0.3V, VBE≈0.7V, IC=β IB. Small changes in IB produce proportional changes in IC, suitable for amplification. Observed at steps 6-10.
• Saturation: Steep region on left where VCE ≤0.1-0.2V, βforced = IC/IB < hFE. Both junctions forward biased, IC limited by RC+RE. Observed at steps 11-12 where VCE=0.07V and 0.02V.

questions.question: What is the exact function of resistor RE in the circuit, and what happens when it is short-circuited?
questions.answer: RE provides negative current feedback for thermal stability. If IC increases due to temperature, VE = IE RE increases. Since VB is fixed by divider, VBE = VB - VE decreases, reducing IB and counteracting rise in IC. When RE is shorted, VE=0V and feedback removed. VBE rises to full divider voltage, IC increases sharply (from 5.25mA to 9.55mA in this experiment) and Q-point moves toward saturation. Circuit becomes vulnerable to thermal runaway and Q-point drift with β variation. This is why RE is standard in practical biasing.

questions.question: Explain the Early Effect (Base-Width Modulation) and its direct physical influence on the slope of the common-emitter output characteristics in the active region.
questions.answer: As VCE (and hence VCB) increases, reverse-biased collector-base depletion region widens, extending mainly into lightly doped base. This reduces effective neutral base width WB. Narrower base means less recombination and steeper minority carrier concentration gradient, so more electrons reach collector and diffusion current increases. Therefore IC shows small positive slope with VCE in active region, rather than perfectly constant. This is modelled by finite output resistance ro = ΔVCE/ΔIC. Extrapolated active-region curves meet at Early voltage VA ≈100V for 2N2222, giving ro ≈ (VA+VCE)/IC ≈105V/5.25mA ≈20kΩ.

questions.question: Design criteria for a "stiff" voltage divider: What engineering condition must the base bias resistors satisfy to render the Q-point completely immune to variations in transistor β?
questions.answer: For Q-point to be independent of β spread (100-300 for 2N2222), divider current must be much larger than base current. Standard rule is Idiv ≥10*IB, equivalent to RTH = RB1||RB2 ≤0.1*(β+1)*RE. When this holds, RTH/(β+1) becomes negligible compared to RE, so IC ≈ (VTH-VBE)/RE, depending only on resistors and VBE, not on β. This is called stiff divider. In this circuit RTH=12.88kΩ, (β+1)RE=15.1kΩ, ratio ~0.85, moderately stiff. Smaller divider resistors would improve stability at cost of higher power dissipation.

learnings: Practical measurement of node voltages VB, VC, VE and calculation of junction voltages VBE, VCE and currents IC, IE from them without direct current measurement.
Ability to identify transistor operating region (cutoff, active, saturation) from VBE and VCE measurements for quick circuit diagnosis.
Understanding how VCC, RC and RE define DC load line and limits of operation, and how to locate Q-point for linear amplification with good headroom.

Appreciation of emitter resistor as feedback element that prevents thermal runaway and stabilizes operating point against β and temperature variations, which is critical in practical amplifier design.
